title: Do heavier objects fall faster?
canonical_question: Do heavier objects fall faster than lighter ones?
summary: Ignoring air resistance, all objects fall with the same acceleration regardless of mass.
A heavier object feels more gravitational force, but it also has more inertia to move, and the two effects cancel exactly.

reuse.rationale: Authored fixture node for the E05 registry.

sections.heading: The surprising answer
sections.body_md: Ignoring air resistance, all objects fall with the same acceleration regardless of mass. A heavy stone and a light one dropped together hit the ground at the same time. The famous intuition that heavier means faster is simply wrong in a vacuum.

sections.heading: Why mass cancels
sections.body_md: A heavier object feels more gravitational force, but it also has more inertia to move, and the two effects cancel exactly. In F = ma the larger force is divided by the larger mass, leaving the same acceleration g. Air resistance, not weight, is what makes a feather lag behind.

key_points: Without air, all masses fall at the same rate.
More weight is offset by more inertia.
Air resistance, not mass, causes real differences.
core.bridge_to_parent: It challenges a misconception tied to the objective’s use of mass.
